![](thumbnail.png)

## Overview

This figure asks whether the same nominal tuition bill became easier or harder to afford for households at different points in the income distribution. It combines the higher-education tuition price series with household income by decile, tracking how the ratio between the two moved for the poorest and richest deciles since 2002.

## Methodology

The tuition-burden index divides the same real tuition-readjustment series used in the IPCA tuition figure by the weighted mean real per-capita household income of each decile, both expressed as 2002 = 100 and both deflated by the same IPCA base. Deciles are computed within each survey year and source; the harmonized series uses PNAD Anual through 2015 and PNAD Contínua from 2016 onward, with 2012–2015 restricted to PNAD Anual observations. Because the burden is a ratio of two indices anchored at the same base year, it says nothing about the absolute affordability of tuition in any single year — only about how a fixed nominal bill moved relative to each decile's own income trajectory since 2002. The underlying tuition series is a fixed-panel readjustment index and does not register the additional compositional cheapening from the post-2015 migration toward distance learning, so the burden shown is, if anything, an upper bound on how much lighter the bill became for lower deciles.

## Reproducibility

**Tier: A**

This pipeline uses only public data, accessible via package/API without any credential (PNADcIBGE, censobr, sidrar, ipeadatar). Run the scripts in `shared-pipeline/` in numeric order to reconstruct the intermediate data.
